The summer I turned sixteen, I rebuilt a two-stroke boat engine with my grandfather. It didn't start. We had spent eleven days on it, and when he pulled the cord the only sound was the rope snapping back against the housing.

He laughed. I didn't. I had a notebook with 43 numbered steps, and I'd followed every one of them.

"Then the mistake is in the notebook," he said, "not in your hands."

It took me a long time to understand why that mattered. I had assumed that being careful and being right were the same thing. They aren't. The notebook was careful. It was also wrong about the fuel mix by a ratio of 50:1, because I had copied it from a manual for a different engine.

We drained the tank the next morning and started again from step 9.
